schema_ddl:
CREATE TABLE EMP (NAME INT, DEPT INT, EMP INT);
CREATE TABLE DEPT (DEPT INT, LOC INT, MGR INT);
q1: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP AS X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT AS Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP AS X, DEPT AS Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP AS X WHERE (X.EMP, X.DEPT) IN (SELECT Y.MGR, Y.DEPT FROM DEPT AS Y WHERE Y.LOC = 3)
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT X.NAME AS XN FROM EMP AS X, DEPT AS Y WHERE X.DEPT = Y.DEPT AND Y.LOC = 3 AND X.EMP = Y.MGR
counterexample: INSERT INTO DEPT (DEPT, LOC, MGR) VALUES (1, 3, 101); INSERT INTO EMP (NAME, DEPT, EMP) VALUES (1, 1, 102);
explanation: Q1 uses a subquery to find the manager of a department located at location 3, and then checks if the employee ID of the employee in the EMP table matches this manager ID for the same department. Q2, on the other hand, directly joins the EMP and DEPT tables on the department ID and checks if the employee ID in the EMP table matches the manager ID in the DEPT table for departments located at location 3. The difference lies in how the conditions are applied and the use of the IN operator in Q1.
counterexample_dsp: The difference in results will be observed when there is a department at location 3 where the employee ID in the EMP table does not match the manager ID in the DEPT table, but the subquery in Q1 still returns true due to the IN operator.
